question: On 16 October 2025, the Commission proposed to expand the Erasmus programme to southern Mediterranean countries, increase mobility, and significantly boost funding. Before presenting this Communication: 1.

Did the Commission verify that the governance structures of the eligible universities comply with the rule of law standards it applies within the EU, including the composition of their governing bodies, the duration of mandates, and possible coolingoff periods?

What measures can the Commission take to ensure these universities do not represent a risk of breaching the principles of the rule of law in a way that could compromise the EU’s sound budget management or protection of its financial interests?
Supporters1
This question is supported by Members other than the authors: Emmanouil Fragkos (ECR), Nikola Bartůšek (PfE).
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (26.2.2026) The Pact for the Mediterranean1 proposes a new ambitious strategy to strengthen EU relations with its southern Mediterranean partners. It aims to invest in people, in growth and mobility, reinforcing the cultural, academic, social, and economic relationships that will make Europe and the region stronger and more resilient.

Short term student exchanges from any region in the world towards the EU, including from the southern Mediterranean, already exist under the international dimension of Erasmus+, financed through the Neighbourhood, Development and International Cooperation Instrument (NDICI – Global Europe).

Universities wishing to participate in Erasmus+ must submit an application that undergoes an evaluation of eligibility and quality. Projects which receive grants are monitored for their continued compliance with the call and grant agreement conditions. Universities which receive a grant must perform their projects according to the highest ethical standards and EU values, including the respect for the rule of law.

The Commission – via Erasmus+ National Agencies and the European Education and Culture Executive Agency – is politically committed and legally bound to ensuring that no one receives EU funding if they are involved in any activities incompatible with EU values, in line with the Financial Regulation2.
Should the Commission become aware of evidence of such activities, it may take appropriate action by excluding the entities concerned from EU financing.
1 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=celex:52025JC0026. 2 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/2509/oj/eng. A 2024 recast of the Financial Regulation includes an
exclusion ground under the Early Detection and Exclusion System for entities engaged in activities contrary to the EU values.
